items.html:
Gum trees (eucalyptus) are by far the most common type of tree in Australia. Their bark is typically light-coloured, with puffy puffy clusters of leaves.

NOTE: Their look may vary significantly, depending on your location within the country. More details can be found in the region-guessing section.

Australian bollards are white, with a red reflector on the front, and a grey reflector on the back.

NOTE: New Zealand uses a bollard where the red reflector wraps around the back, meaning the reflector goes from end to end while the Australian one stops in the middle.

Australia drives on the left.

NOTE: A handful of other countries also drive on the left. See this infographic for more information.

Australia uses almost exclusively white road lines, with a few rare exceptions in alpine regions such as Mount Kosciuszko and Mount Hotham.

NOTE: If you are considering guessing in Australia, but see yellow outside lines or a yellow middle line, you will probably be in South Africa or New Zealand respectively. Note that New Zealand can have all white road lines as well.

Outside lines in Australia sometimes feature rumble strips that look like small white stripes perpendicular to the road line.

NOTE: Northern Territory roads very rarely have rumble strips.

!!In addition, you can find similar rumble strips in New Zealand.

Give-way signs in Australia have a white border and black text.

NOTE: New Zealand’s give-way signs use red, instead of black, text. Give-way signs are very rarely seen in South Africa.

Australia uses white on black and black on yellow chevrons.

NOTE: Chevrons in New Zealand use the same colours, but the yellow ones will have a thin black border and often, a speed limit.

Green signs with white arrows on either side can be seen at intersections which show nearby towns or cities. A number indicating the number of kilometres away the town can sometimes be seen.

NOTE: Whereas Australian highways have alphanumeric names (e.g. A2, C222), highways in New Zealand are represented as a number on a red crest.

Australian speed limit signs have black text in a red circle on a large white rectangle.

NOTE: New Zealand speed limit signs normally do not have the white rectangular background.
A long antenna can be seen in Generation 3 coverage.
Different states use different licence plate designs, which can be somewhat visible through the blur.
Australian phone numbers are 8 digits with a 2-digit area code in front. A map of these by state can be seen here. Keep in mind, not all phone numbers will include an area code in front of it.

Each state has a unique bus stop design. These are quite common in urban rounds, so are worth learning. Darwin bus stops are usually concrete shelters.

NOTE: The designs may vary slightly, but should still be recognisable. There are multiple versions of Tasmanian bus stops, but most of them should have the word ‘metro’ on it.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

The area around Warramboo in SA to Madura in WA has a unique landscape. Vegetation is quite dry and is made up of shrubs and wide crowned eucalyptus. In addition, the soil is sandy with a slight orange tint.

The dry area east of Adelaide and into northwestern Victoria has a similar landscape, with the same vegetation but usually with whiter soil.

NOTE: The soil gets more red in the WA side. Redder soil can also be seen more inland on the Victorian side around Mildura. In addition, the Nullarbor Highway has a distinct landscape.

Lush green or golden fields can be found in this band from the south of the Yorke Peninsula to Echuca. In the SA side, the landscape should be drier than the Victorian side and more wide crowned eucalyptus can be seen. On the Victorian side, the trees generally have more leaves and are taller.

NOTE: The area near Mount Gambier has a distinct landscape. For more information, see below.
Coastal northern Queensland is very tropical. Typical vegetation consists of palm trees and dark green vegetation.

The landscape in inland NSW is mostly flat, and the soil gets redder the more inland you go. Vegetation consists of mostly dry pale-green shrubs. Further east and on the Queensland and Victorian borders, the climate gets more temperate but is still quite dry and more eucalyptus trees can be seen, with the soil transitioning into a more sandy colour as well as more hills being visible.
The vegetation in the area surrounding Darwin is extremely distinct. It features dark red soil, as well as rich green grass and trees. The tree trunks are typically black.

Tasmania has a cool temperate climate which is uncommon in the rest of Australia and is comparable to central-southern Chile or New Zealand. Typical landscape consists of green rolling hills that can look dry in winter coverage. Eucalyptus trees can be seen on the side of roads and on hills in the distance. Rural Tasmania is also quite hilly with dense eucalyptus forests making up the landscape.

NOTE: Certain areas of Victoria can look similar so make sure to look for other clues.
Termite mounds can sometimes be seen in the Northern Territory and rarely northern WA and QLD. They appear as brown, spiky formations rising out of the ground.
These brush plants are commonly seen in Western Australia.

Sugarcane plantations are very common in Northern Queensland, due to its tropical climate.

NOTE: Sugarcane plantations can be seen as far south as northern NSW, however are most commonly found in northern Queensland. For a detailed overview, see this map.

The iconic Stobie pole, made of steel and concrete, is specific to South Australia. The pole tops (trident or rotated letter “E”) are also unique.

NOTE: A few thousand of these poles can be found in other states, most notably Tasmania.

These rusty metal poles, containing several holes, are unique to the Northern Territory.

NOTE: These poles can also sometimes be found in some areas of northern WA, such as Wyndham.
According to a 2006 review, 64% of all concrete poles are located in the state of Victoria.

A trident-like pole top can sometimes be seen in Western Australia and Victoria. In Western Australia, the pole will often have red insulators and black paint on the crossbar (shown in the image).

For the meta to work, all 3 insulators must be connected to the crossbar. This link shows a similar looking pole that is incorrect, as the middle insulator is connected to the pole itself rather than to the crossbar.
Queensland features these unique pole tops with coils that are angled upwards on the sides.
Victorian pole tops feature 3 circular coils; 2 on the sides, and 1 vertical one at the top. At times, other extensions can be seen on these poles.

Poletops in Tasmania often consist of a thin metal crossbar bent 90 degrees to form an L-shape.

NOTE: Regular Australian crossbars are usually made out of wood.

Circular blue stickers can be found on Queensland poles. You may occasionally see the same type of sticker in a different colour, or with the colour almost completely faded.

NOTE: Blue stickers can also be found on French poles.
These black markings are specific to electricity poles in the region encompassing the cities of Gold Coast, Brisbane, and Sunshine Coast in Queensland. They are often accompanied by diagonal numbers.

Olive-green possum guards are only found on electricity poles in Tasmania.

NOTE: Possum guards are found all over Australia. The colour is what distinguishes them.
Poles in Western Australia often have green painted bases, and sometimes a white sticker or a red and white band attached.

Reflectors that are shorter in height than the regular ones are most common in Queensland and South Australia.

NOTE: This is most consistent with 4 or more short reflectors visible in the round. A low amount of short reflectors is less consistent. This is not consistent in Generation 2.

Bollards with brown paint at the bottom are most commonly found in Western Australia.

NOTE: Brown paint at the bottom of exposed bollards can also rarely be seen in other states, however the brown section will not be as large.
These black-and-white stripy bollards are unique to Western Australia.
This black-and-yellow bollard is exclusive to Queensland.

Yellow signposts are specific to Western Australia.

NOTE: Although South Australia does not use yellow signposts for regular road signs, SA bus stops will have yellow posts.

Some signposts in South Australia and Western Australia are flat rather than round.

NOTE: These signposts are usually yellow in Western Australia.
Signposts in the Northern Territory can feature these yellow stickers.
Road signs with a fluorescent border are almost exclusively found in Queensland.

New South Wales is the only state to use red ‘No Stopping’ signs.

NOTE: All other states use white versions.
The white ‘No Stopping’ and ‘No Parking’ signs that include text are unique to the Australian Capital Territory.
White directional signs can only be found in Tasmania.

Roads that start with the letter ‘C’ are only found in Victoria and Tasmania. In addition, South Australia has some C roads near the border with Victoria.

NOTE: Since these are smaller and less major roads, Generation 1 or 2 is common.
Within Australia, a speed limit of 130 km/h can only be found in the Northern Territory.
Some ‘Keep Left’ signs in New South Wales, Queensland, and the Northern Territory use this thinner version, which does not include an arrow.

Traffic lights with a white outline around the frame are found in the eastern and western states of WA, QLD, NSW, ACT and Tas. Traffic lights without a border are found in the remaining, central states.
You can find these dark green property markers on the sides of roads in Western Australia.
You can find these white property markers on the sides of roads in South Australia.
This guardrail ending, featuring a black dash on a yellow background, is almost exclusive to New South Wales and the ACT.
You can find these white hydrant poles that feature a blue circle and a red section on top of it in Victoria.
These fire hydrants with red painted tops are unique to Victoria.
Generation 2 cannot be found in the Northern Territory.

Australia is home to dozens of rare Google cars, which can usually be found in natural reserves.

Most rare Google cars with snorkels are located in New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory. The snorkels are dark grey or black extensions to the side of the car, to keep the engine dry when submerged in water.

NOTE: The only snorkels outside NSW and ACT are found on two cars in Western Australia (1 and 2).

_GeoHints has a complete overview of all rare cars, which can be found on this page._

For country streak purposes, Christmas Island and Cocos (Keeling) Islands are counted as part of Australia. For example, clicking Australia on Christmas Island counts as a country streak.

These islands have unique cars which makes them easily identifiable.

_Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Christmas Island here._

_Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Cocos (Keeling) Islands here._
The area around Tom Price can be recognized by its red soil, Generation 2 camera and rocky hills.
Alice Springs, an isolated town in the southern part of the Northern Territory, features distinct orange rocks that can be seen in the distance or at the end of roads.

The northern QLD city of Cairns is distinct due to its tropical vegetation and big green mountains around the city.

NOTE: To differentiate Cairns from other northern Queensland towns, Cairns has many high rise buildings and should feel quite urban. Divided roads are also common in downtown Cairns, and only commonly seen in Mackay further south, where it is less tropical and more flat.
The Grampians are isolated hills that are viewable from afar within the otherwise flat western Victorian agricultural landscape.
The area around Mount Gambier, SA features white soil and extensive pine tree plantations, making it recognisable.

Kangaroo Island in South Australia tends to have a distinct look. The vegetation mostly consists of bushes and low, stubby eucalyptus trees with puffy clusters of leaves. The orange soil colour is reminiscent of Western Australia.

In addition, the island only has Generation 2, and Generation 4 coverage.
The Stirling Ranges are a small mountain range in Western Australia that tower over a largely flat plain, such that they can be viewed from a distance.

The Nullarbor Highway (Latin for “no tree”) can be easily recognized thanks to the flatness, overall grey look and very low vegetation.

NOTE: Use the road angle or road lines to determine whether you are on the WA or SA side.
On most of the Northern Territory section of the Barkly Highway and a small part of the Queensland section, a wire can be seen on the left side of the car.
Dorat Road (23) in the Northern Territory can be easily recognized thanks to its distinct Darwin area landscape and lack of road lines.

The Sturt Highway from Wentworth to Wagga Wagga can have triple broken centre lines.

NOTE: Triple broken centre lines can also be found on other major roads in NSW, such as the Gwydir Highway. However, they are most common on the Sturt Highway.

The Stuart Highway from Alice Springs to around Pimba, SA can be easily recognized by its bright orange dirt, short trees and blue car Generation 4.

NOTE: Use the road angle and whether there are rumble strips to determine whether you are in NT or SA. Rumble strips are much rarer on the NT side.
Melbourne poles commonly feature these white, rectangular stickers, with a smaller blue square inside it.

All-yellow road lines can be seen on roads around Mount Kosciuszko.

In addition, a unique white truck with a snorkel, and cab guard can be found.

NOTE: All yellow road lines can also be found in other alpine areas in Victoria and New South Wales, so make sure to look at the landscape and other clues.
South Australian style Stobie poles can sometimes be found in the NSW town of Broken Hill.
This street sign is unique to Brisbane City Council.
This street sign is unique to Gold Coast City Council.
This street sign is unique to the City of Sydney.

steps.html:
GeoGuessr’s own official Australia map is not very good, for a variety of reasons. Plonk It recommends the following map instead:

  • A Balanced Australia (map link) - Well balanced, computer generated map with 80k+ locations across Australia and some select few in Cocos and Christmas Island. Used for the Australia record categories on the official Plonk It leaderboard.

In addition, here are some resources to help you practise Australia:

  • Plonk It Australia (map link) - This map contains locations for practising each meta in the Plonk It Australia guide from step 2 to 3.

lm.name: Agriculture - Sugarcane
lm.note: Sugarcane plantations are very common in Northern Queensland, due to its tropical climate.

lm.name: Car Meta - Open Trunk Meta
lm.note: The town of Gascoyne Junction in Western Australia is distinct, as the driver left the car boot open while covering this town, creating a very unique car meta.

lm.name: Car Meta - Snorkel Car
lm.note:
Australia is home to dozens of rare Google cars, which can usually be found in natural reserves.

Most rare Google cars with snorkels are located in New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory. The only snorkel cars outside of NSW are in the northwestern part of Wunaamin Conservation Area (northern WA) and along Lucky Bay (south coastal WA).

lm.name: Car Meta - Wire Car Meta
lm.note: On most of the Northern Territory section of the Barkly Highway and a small part of the Queensland section, a wire can be seen on the left side of the car.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Gen 2
lm.note: Generation 2 coverage cannot be found in Northern Territory. It can also help in 50/50s between Victoria and Tasmania, where Gen 2 is more common in Tasmania.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Gen 2 Twig Meta
lm.note: In Generation 2 coverage in an area of Eastern NSW, a twig is visible in the Generation 2 halo.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Gen 2 Whole Leaf
lm.note: In a lot of Generation 2 around the towns of Morwell and Traralgon in Eastern Victoria, an entire leaf is visible in the Generation 2 halo. A version with only the top half of a leaf can also be seen in eastern SA.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Half Leaf
lm.note: The upper half of a leaf can sometimes be seen on the Generation 2 halo in southeastern South Australia. If it's an entire leaf, it is in Eastern Victoria.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Jervis Bay Meta
lm.note: Jervis Bay only has Gen 1 coverage, all of which has a 2021 copyright.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Smoke Coverage
lm.note: Around the Devils Marbles, north of Davenport in the Northern Territory, smoke from a bushfire is visible.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Splodgey Sun
lm.note: A sun with "splodges" around it can be observed on the 95 in Western Australia, between Newman and Ex Doolgunna.

lm.name: Infrastructure - ∀-Poletop - Round
lm.note: The ∀-Poletop is found in South Australia and New South Wales. In SA, the pole will be a stobie pole, while in NSW it will be round.

lm.name: Infrastructure - 130 km/h speed limit
lm.note: Within Australia, a speed limit of 130 km/h can only be found in the Northern Territory.

lm.name: Infrastructure - 25 school zone
lm.note: South Australia is the only Australian state that uses a 25 speed limit in school zones.

lm.name: Infrastructure - 90° poletop
lm.note: Poletops in Tasmania often consist of a thin metal crossbar bent 90 degrees to form an L-shape.

lm.name: Infrastructure - ACT Bus Stop
lm.note: Unique to Australian Capital Territory (Canberra).

lm.name: Infrastructure - Black pole marking
lm.note:
These black markings are specific to electricity poles in Queensland. They are often accompanied by diagonal numbers.

They are almost exclusively found between Gold Coast and Sunshine Coast

lm.name: Infrastructure - black-white striped bollard
lm.note: These black-and-white stripy bollards are unique to Western Australia.

lm.name: Infrastructure - black-yellow striped bollard
lm.note: This black-and-yellow bollard is exclusive to Queensland.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Blue Square on Pole
lm.note: Melbourne poles commonly feature these white, rectangular stickers, with a smaller blue square inside it.

lm.name: Infrastructure - bollard with brown bottom
lm.note: Bollards with brown paint at the bottom are most commonly found in Western Australia.

lm.name: Infrastructure - bollard with short reflector
lm.note: Reflectors that are shorter than the regular ones are most common in Queensland and South Australia.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Brisbane Streetsign
lm.note: Identified by the little symbol.

lm.name: Infrastructure - C-Road
lm.note: Roads that start with the letter ‘C’ are only found in Victoria and Tasmania. In addition, South Australia has some C roads near the border with Victoria.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Charters Towers Red Roads
lm.note: As a general rule in Queensland state, Australia, red tinted roads are found mostly around Charters Towers (especially when you have more trees), they can also be found on the A2 near label, and the 1 further north. These areas are indicated in the distribution, but there may be minor exceptions.

lm.name: Infrastructure - concrete pole
lm.note: According to a 2006 review, 64% of all concrete poles are located in the state of Victoria.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Darwin Bus Stop
lm.note: The city of Darwin, NT uses concrete shelters as bus stops.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Dorat Road
lm.note: Dorat Road (23) in the Northern Territory can be easily recognized thanks to its distinct Darwin area landscape and lack of road lines.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Dotted Concrete Pole
lm.note: These round concrete poles with dots going up on them are found in New South Wales.

lm.name: Infrastructure - flat signpost
lm.note: Some signposts in South Australia and Western Australia are flat rather than round.

lm.name: Infrastructure - fluoresecent sign border
lm.note: Road signs with a fluorescent border are almost exclusively found in Queensland.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Gold Coast Streetsign
lm.note: This street sign is unique to Gold Coast City Council.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Green Dot on Pole
lm.note: This Green Dot on poles is sometimes found in New South Wales.

lm.name: Infrastructure - green pole bottom
lm.note: Poles in Western Australia often have green painted bases, and sometimes a white sticker or a red and white band attached.

lm.name: Infrastructure - green property marker
lm.note: You can find these dark green property markers on the sides of roads in Western Australia.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Hanging Insulator
lm.note: These poles with hanging insulators are found in Queensland and New South Wales.

lm.name: Infrastructure - hydrant with blue circle
lm.note: You can find these white hydrant poles that feature a blue circle and a red section on top of it in Victoria.

lm.name: Infrastructure - hydrant with red top
lm.note: These fire hydrants with red painted tops are unique to Victoria.

lm.name: Infrastructure - License Plate - Slim NSW
lm.note: Very slim license plate (similar to Swiss front plates) are found in Victoria and New South Wales. While in Victoria, you can usually see two blue blocks of texts, in NSW they appear plain.

lm.name: Infrastructure - License Plate - Slim Victoria
lm.note: Very slim license plate (similar to Swiss front plates) are found in Victoria and New South Wales. While in Victoria, you can usually see two blue blocks of texts, in NSW they appear plain.

lm.name: Infrastructure - License Plate - Taxi - Blue
lm.note: Blue plates on Taxis are found exclusively in New South Wales.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Mount Kosciuszko
lm.note:
All-yellow road lines can be seen on roads around Mount Kosciuszko.

In addition, a unique white truck with a snorkel, and cab guard can be found.

lm.name: Infrastructure - No-Stopping-sign with text
lm.note: The white ‘No Stopping’ and ‘No Parking’ signs that include text are unique to the Australian Capital Territory.

lm.name: Infrastructure - NSW Bus Stop
lm.note: New South Wales uses these two designs for bus stops. One is blue and has a white B in a circle with it, the other has the signpost bending over the actual sign.

lm.name: Infrastructure - NSW guardrail ending
lm.note: This guardrail ending, featuring a black dash on a yellow background, is almost exclusive to New South Wales and the ACT.

lm.name: Infrastructure - NT License Plate
lm.note: License Plates in Northern Territory have bright red lettering which shines through the blur. Looks kind of similar to the Queensland plates, which are a bit darker.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Octagonal Pole
lm.note: Octagonal Poles in Australia are found mostly in and around Sydney.

lm.name: Infrastructure - olive-green possum guard
lm.note: Olive-green possum guards are only found on electricity poles in Tasmania.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Poletag - H
lm.note: The 'H' poletag is found in New South Wales.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Poletag - HP
lm.note: This poletag with 'HP' is found in New South Wales.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Poletag - NSW - Horizontal
lm.note: Within New South Wales, purely horizontal poletags (i.e. no vertical on the same pole), are not found around Sydney.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Poletag - NSW - Letter Code
lm.note: In NSW, poletags in the triangle formed by Sydney, Newcastle and Scone (view map) almost always have one or two letters in their codes.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Poletag - NSW - Vertical / Outer White
lm.note: Within NSW, these vertical plates with white ends are not found near Sydney. Note that otherwise, vertical plates will be close to Sydney within NSW.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Poletag - QLD - Vertical
lm.note: Poletags with a blue sticker, and a vertical steel tag are found in Queensland, north of Rockhampton.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Poletag - Vertical / Regular
lm.note:
Within NSW, regular vertical poletags are found south and west of Sydney.

Note that if the poletags have white ends on each side, they are NOT close to Sydney, but rather throughout the rest of NSW.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Poletag - Yellow T
lm.note: This poletag which consists of rectangular yellow stickers that usually form a T, is exclusive to New South Wales.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Queensland Bus Stop
lm.note: Bus stops in Queensland have a yellow signpost bending over the actual sign.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Queensland License Plate
lm.note: The Queensland License Plate has dark red letters which can shine through the blur. Looks similar to the NT plate, which has a lighter red tone. There is also an old, green version, which could theoretically show up.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Queensland poletop
lm.note: Queensland features these unique pole tops with coils that are angled upwards on the sides.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Queensland sticker
lm.note: Circular blue stickers can be found on Queensland poles. You may occasionally see the same type of sticker in a different colour, or with the colour almost completely faded.

lm.name: Infrastructure - red "No Stopping" sign
lm.note: New South Wales is the only state to use red ‘No Stopping’ signs.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Roadline Gap with no Reflector
lm.note: In South Australia and the ACT, you can sometimes find gaps in the outer roadlines. If this gap has no reflector, it is South Australia.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Roadline gap with Reflector
lm.note: In South Australia and the ACT, you can sometimes find gaps in the outer roadlines. In ACT, there will always be a reflector in the gap. This can also appear occasionally in South Australia.

lm.name: Infrastructure - rusty holey pole
lm.note: These rusty metal poles, containing several holes, are unique to the Northern Territory, and rarely the northern part of Western Australia.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Sloped Kerbs
lm.note: You can sometimes see sloped kerbs in Perth, where it gradually declines to the road, whilst in other cities kerbs go straight down at a 90 degree angle.

lm.name: Infrastructure - South Australia Bus Stop
lm.note: Orange signpost, sign extending over the signpost.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Stobie pole
lm.note: The iconic Stobie pole, made of steel and concrete, is specific to South Australia. Outside of SA, it sometimes occurs in Broken Hill, NSW or Tasmania.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Sydney Streetsign
lm.note: This street sign is unique to the City of Sydney.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Tasmania Bus Stop
lm.note: Different versions, but usually have "Metro" written on them.

lm.name: Infrastructure - thin "Keep Left" sign
lm.note: Some ‘Keep Left’ signs in New South Wales, Queensland, and the Northern Territory use this thinner version, which does not include an arrow.

lm.name: Infrastructure - traffic light with no outline
lm.note: Traffic lights without a border are found in Northern Territory, South Australia and Victoria.

lm.name: Infrastructure - traffic light with white outline
lm.note: Traffic lights with a white outline around the frame are found in the eastern and western states of WA, QLD, NSW, ACT and Tas. Traffic lights without a border are found in the remaining, central states.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Triple Broken Roadlines
lm.note: The Sturt Highway from Wentworth to Wagga Wagga can have triple broken centre lines. They can also be found on other major roads in NSW, such as the Gwydir Highway.

lm.name: Infrastructure - upward pointing trident pole
lm.note: A trident-like pole top with the insulators pointing to the top can sometimes be seen in Western Australia and Victoria.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Victoria Bus Stop
lm.note: Bus Stops in Victoria can be recognized by their color scheme: White-Orange-Black-Grey-White.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Victoria License Plate
lm.note: License plates in Victoria have a little small triangle at the top, which can sometimes be recognized through the blur.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Victoria poletop
lm.note: Victorian pole tops feature 3 circular coils; 2 on the sides, and 1 vertical one at the top. At times, other extensions can be seen on these poles.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Western Australia Bus Stop
lm.note: Bus Stops in Australia are marked by these horizontal poles with information on them.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Western Australia License Plate
lm.note: Western Australian License Plate have blue letters and a thin blue stripe at the top, which can sometimes be recognized through the blur.

lm.name: Infrastructure - white directional sign
lm.note: White directional signs can only be found in Tasmania.

lm.name: Infrastructure - white property marker
lm.note: You can find these white property markers on the sides of roads in South Australia.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Yellow License Plate
lm.note: Yellow license plates can occasionally be found in New South Wales. Most license plates are still white, though. The old design of Western Australian plates is also yellow, so you might stumble upon them in WA very rarely.

lm.name: Infrastructure - yellow signpost
lm.note: Yellow signposts are specific to Western Australia.

lm.name: Infrastructure - ш-shaped poletop
lm.note: Poletops that resemble the cyrillic letter ш are unique to South Australia.

lm.name: Landscape - Alice Springs
lm.note: Alice Springs, an isolated town in the southern part of the Northern Territory, features distinct orange rocks that can be seen in the distance or at the end of roads.

lm.name: Landscape - Cairns Landscape
lm.note: The northern QLD city of Cairns is distinct due to its tropical vegetation and big green mountains around the city.

lm.name: Landscape - Darwin Landscape
lm.note: The vegetation in the area surrounding Darwin is extremely distinct. It features dark red soil, as well as rich green grass and trees. The tree trunks are typically black.

lm.name: Landscape - Eastern South Australia Landscape
lm.note:
The dry area east of Adelaide and into northwestern Victoria has quite dry vegetation and is made up of shrubs and wide cronwed eucalyptus. In addition, the soil is sandy with a white tint.

Western South Australia has a similar landscape, but with orangish soil.

lm.name: Landscape - Green & Golden Fields
lm.note: Lush green or golden fields can be found in this band from the south of the Yorke Peninsula to Echuca. In the SA side, the landscape should be drier than the Victorian side and more wide crowned eucalyptus can be seen. On the Victorian side, the trees generally have more leaves and are taller.

lm.name: Landscape - Inland New South Wales Landscape
lm.note: The landscape in inland NSW is mostly flat, and the soil gets redder the more inland you go. Vegetation consists of mostly dry pale-green shrubs. Further east and on the Queensland and Victorian borders, the climate gets more temperate but is still quite dry and more eucalyptus trees can be seen, with the soil transitioning into a more sandy colour as well as more hills being visible.

lm.name: Landscape - Kangaroo Island Landscape
lm.note:
Kangaroo Island in South Australia tends to have a distinct look. The vegetation mostly consists of bushes and low, stubby eucalyptus trees with puffy clusters of leaves. The orange soil colour is reminiscent of Western Australia.

In addition, the island only has Generation 2 and Generation 4 coverage, with Generation 2 being most common.

lm.name: Landscape - Mount Gambier Tree Plantations
lm.note: The area around Mount Gambier, SA features white soil and extensive pine tree plantations, making it recognisable.

lm.name: Landscape - Northern Queensland Landscape
lm.note: Coastal northern Queensland is very tropical. Typical vegetation consists of palm trees and dark green vegetation.

lm.name: Landscape - Nullarbor Highway
lm.note:
The Nullarbor Highway (Latin for “no tree”) can be easily recognized thanks to the flatness, overall grey look and very low vegetation.

NOTE: Use the road angle or road lines to determine whether you are on the WA or SA side.

lm.name: Landscape - Reddish-Orange Soil
lm.note: Western Australia, and especially the Perth area, is known for its reddish-orange soil.

lm.name: Landscape - Stuart Highway with Blue Car
lm.note: The Stuart Highway from Alice Springs to around Pimba, SA can be easily recognized by its bright orange dirt, short trees and blue car Generation 4.

lm.name: Landscape - Tasmania Landscape
lm.note: Tasmania has a cool temperate climate which is uncommon in the rest of Australia and is comparable to central-southern Chile or New Zealand. Typical landscape consists of green rolling hills that can look dry in winter coverage. Eucalyptus trees can be seen on the side of roads and on hills in the distance. Rural Tasmania is also quite hilly with dense eucalyptus forests making up the landscape.

lm.name: Landscape - Termite Hills
lm.note: Termite mounds can sometimes be seen in the Northern Territory and rarely northern WA and QLD. They appear as brown, spiky formations rising out of the ground.

lm.name: Landscape - Tom Price Landscape
lm.note: The area around Tom Price can be recognized by its red soil and rocky hills.

lm.name: Landscape - Western South Australia Landscape
lm.note:
The area around Warramboo in SA to Madura in WA has a unique landscape. Vegetation is quite dry and is made up of shrubs and wide crowned eucalyptus. In addition, the soil is sandy with a slight orange tint.

The dry area east of Adelaide and into northwestern Victoria has a similar landscape, with the same vegetation but usually with whiter soil.

lm.note: These brush plants are commonly seen in Western Australia.

lm.name: Vegetation - Queensland Fan Palm
lm.note: The Queensland fan palm or Australian fan palm, is a species endemic to northeastern Queensland, Australia (Specially around Cairns).

lm.name: Vegetation - Sand Palm
lm.note: The sand palm is endemic to the north of the Northern Territory of Australia, from the Fitzmaurice River to Cape Arnhem and inland as far as Katherine.

lm.name: Christmas Island
lm.note: Most of Christmas Island is covered by dense tropical forest. Some unpaved roads feature bright, white sandy soil. A small part of the coverage is in built-up areas. And in some places, palms can be seen.

lm.name: Coastal Queensland
lm.note: Coastal northern Queensland is very tropical. Typical vegetation consists of palm trees and dark green vegetation.

lm.name: Cocos Islands
lm.note: The general landscape consists of bright white sand, many palms and mowed grass. Cocos Islands is significantly less forested or hilly compared to Christmas Island.

lm.name: Darwin
lm.note: The vegetation in the area surrounding Darwin is extremely distinct. It features dark red soil, as well as rich green grass and trees. The tree trunks are typically black.

lm.name: Inland New South Wales
lm.note: The landscape in inland NSW is mostly flat, and the soil gets redder the more inland you go. Vegetation consists of mostly dry pale-green shrubs. Further east and on the Queensland and Victorian borders, the climate gets more temperate but is still quite dry and more eucalyptus trees can be seen, with the soil transitioning into a more sandy colour as well as more hills being visible.

lm.name: Kangaroo Island
lm.note: Kangaroo Island in South Australia tends to have a distinct look. The vegetation mostly consists of bushes and low, stubby eucalyptus trees with puffy clusters of leaves. The orange soil colour is reminiscent of Western Australia.

lm.name: South Fields
lm.note: Lush green or golden fields can be found in this band from the south of the Yorke Peninsula to Echuca. In the SA side, the landscape should be drier than the Victorian side and more wide crowned eucalyptus can be seen. On the Victorian side, the trees generally have more leaves and are taller.

lm.name: Southwest South Australia Landscape
lm.note:
The area around Warramboo in SA to Madura in WA has a unique landscape. Vegetation is quite dry and is made up of shrubs and wide crowned eucalyptus. In addition, the soil is sandy with a slight orange tint. The dry area east of Adelaide and into northwestern Victoria has a similar landscape, with the same vegetation but usually with whiter soil.

NOTE: The soil gets more red in the WA side. Redder soil can also be seen more inland on the Victorian side around Mildura.

lm.name: Tasmania
lm.note:
Tasmania has a cool temperate climate which is uncommon in the rest of Australia and is comparable to central-southern Chile or New Zealand. Typical landscape consists of green rolling hills that can look dry in winter coverage. Eucalyptus trees can be seen on the side of roads and on hills in the distance. Rural Tasmania is also quite hilly with dense eucalyptus forests making up the landscape.

NOTE: Certain areas of Victoria can look similar so make sure to look for other clues.

lm.name: Tom Price Hills
lm.note: The area around Tom Price can be recognized by its red soil and rocky hills.

lm.name: Western Australia
lm.note:
Western Australia, and especially the Perth area, is known for its reddish-orange soil.

NOTE: Although this is very useful, there are numerous areas in WA with light soil, and conversely there are areas in other states with reddish-orange soil.

lm.name: ACT Plate
lm.note: The ACT plate features equally sized blue sections on both sides with a white area in the center. This symmetry helps distinguish it from the Tasmania plate, which has more blue concentrated on the right side. For comparison, Tasmania plate on next slide.

lm.name: NSW Plate
lm.note: The easiest to recognize is the New South Wales plate, which appears purely yellow when blurred, making it easily identifiable even from a distance.

lm.name: NSW Plate – Black and White
lm.note: The New South Wales black and white plate appears slightly darker than the South Australia plate when blurred. Since both can look similar, pay attention to the surroundings—yellow plates are more common in NSW. For comparison, SA plate on next slide.

lm.name: NT Plate
lm.note: The Northern Territory plate features a bright red text on white design, similar to Queensland’s, but in a slightly lighter red. For distinction, look at the surroundings — the NT often has dry, reddish soil and sparse vegetation, giving off a distinct outback vibe compared to Queensland’s greener and more tropical feel. For comparison, Queensland plate on next slide.

lm.name: Queensland Plate
lm.note: The Queensland plate is very similar to the Northern Territory one, but uses a darker shade of red. For distinction, rely on the surrounding environment — Queensland usually feels more humid and lush, while the Northern Territory tends to look drier and more outback-like. For comparison, NT plate on next slide.

lm.name: SA Plate
lm.note: The South Australia plate is purely black and white. When blurred, it often appears black on the sides with a small white 'dot' in the center, though in certain lighting conditions it can also look entirely white. It can look like the black and white NSW plate but in a lighter white when blurred: For comparison, NSW plate on next slide.

lm.name: Tasmania Plate
lm.note: The Tasmania plate typically has more blue concentrated on the right side, while the ACT plate shows symmetrical blue sections on both sides. This subtle difference can help tell them apart when the image is blurred. For comparison, ACT plate on next slide.

lm.name: Victoria Plate
lm.note: The Victoria plate is easy to recognize thanks to its distinctive blue triangle in the center, which appears as a blue dot in the upper middle of the plate when blurred.

lm.name: WA Plate
lm.note: One of the easiest to recognize is the Western Australia plate, which features a blue horizontal bar across the top. This element remains clearly visible even when the plate is blurred.

lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note: • Australia uses almost exclusively white road lines, with a few rare exceptions in alpine regions such as Mount Kosciuszko and Mount Hotham.

lm.name: Roadlines #2
lm.note:
• Outside lines in Australia sometimes feature rumble strips that look like small white stripes perpendicular to the road line.

--- NOTE:

  • Northern Territory roads very rarely have rumble strips.
  • In addition, you can find similar rumble strips in New Zealand.

lm.name: angled upwards
lm.note: Queensland features these unique pole tops with coils that are angled upwards on the sides.

lm.name: black markings
lm.note: These black markings are specific to electricity poles in Queensland. They are often accompanied by diagonal numbers.

lm.name: blue circular sticker
lm.note:
Circular blue stickers can be found on Queensland poles. You may occasionally see the same type of sticker in a different colour, or with the colour almost completely faded.

NOTE: Blue stickers can also be found on French poles.

lm.name: blue square
lm.note: Melbourne poles commonly feature these white, rectangular stickers, with a smaller blue square inside it.

lm.name: concret pole
lm.note: According to a 2006 review, 64% of all concrete poles are located in the state of Victoria.

lm.name: marking bands
lm.note: Poles in Western Australia often have green painted bases, and sometimes a white sticker or a red and white band attached.

lm.name: rusty metal pole
lm.note:
These rusty metal poles, containing several holes, are unique to the Northern Territory.

NOTE: These poles can also sometimes be found in some areas of northern WA, such as Wyndham.

lm.name: stobie pole
lm.note:
The iconic Stobie pole, made of steel and concrete, is specific to South Australia. The pole tops (trident or rotated letter “E”) are also unique.

NOTE: A few thousand of these poles can be found in other states, most notably Tasmania.

lm.name: tas pole
lm.note:
Poletops in Tasmania often consist of a thin metal crossbar bent 90 degrees to form an L-shape.

NOTE: Regular Australian crossbars are usually made out of wood.

lm.name: trident pole
lm.note: A trident-like pole top can sometimes be seen in Western Australia and Victoria.

lm.name: victoria pole
lm.note: Victorian pole tops feature 3 circular coils; 2 on the sides, and 1 vertical one at the top. At times, other extensions can be seen on these poles.

Australian bollards are white, with a red reflector on the front, and a grey reflector on the back.
